title: Touching intervals
options: Yes — 3 <= 3, they share the point 3 and merge to [1, 5]
explanation: With <= the shared endpoint counts as overlap (LeetCode's Merge Intervals wants this). Meeting-room problems sometimes want strict < — read the problem's definition every time.

title: Drill: can attend all meetings?
prompt: From memory: given meeting intervals, return whether one person can attend them all (no two overlap; touching endpoints like [1,3],[3,5] are OK). Sort by start, then check each consecutive pair.

solution.explanation: After sorting by start, if meeting i overlaps any earlier meeting, it overlaps meeting i-1, so checking neighbors is enough. This is LeetCode's Meeting Rooms. O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space (beyond the sort).

hints: Checking every pair is O(n²). What order would make only neighbors able to conflict?
Sort by start with `Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])`, then compare each meeting with the one before it.
Conflict iff `intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]`. Use strict `<` because touching is allowed.

title: Drill: count merged intervals
prompt: From memory (sort then sweep): return how many intervals remain after merging all overlaps. Sort by start, then sweep tracking the current merged end.

solution.explanation: Sorting by start means an interval can only extend the most recent group. A start beyond that group's end begins a new one. The `max` keeps a contained interval from shrinking the end. O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.

hints: After sorting by start, which merged group can the next interval possibly join?
Only the current (last) group. Track its end while you sweep.
If `intervals[i][0] > end`, a new group starts (`count++`). Otherwise `end = Math.max(end, intervals[i][1])`.

title: Why sort by end?
prompt: For Non-overlapping Intervals (remove the fewest so the rest don't overlap), the greedy sorts by **end** and keeps each compatible interval. Why end and not start?
options: The interval that finishes earliest leaves the most room for the rest. Sorting by start could keep a long early interval like [1,100] that blocks many short ones
There's no difference. Either order gives the same count
explanation: Exchange argument: in any optimal set, swap the first interval for the earliest-ending one. It ends no later, so everything after it still fits. For [[1,100],[2,3],[4,5]], start order keeps [1,100] and removes 2 intervals, while end order keeps [2,3] and [4,5] and removes only 1.

title: Recall: Meeting Rooms II heap
prompt: Fill in the min-heap-of-end-times template for the minimum number of meeting rooms.
explanation: Sort by start with `Integer.compare` (no subtraction overflow). `peek()` is the room that frees up soonest. If it's free by this start, `poll()` to reuse it. Always `offer` this meeting's end. The heap size is the peak number of simultaneous meetings.
